Family Health

When sexual behaviour feels out of control: assessment and support

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

If sexual behaviour repeatedly feels beyond your control and is disrupting your life, support is available. The first step is a careful assessment that respects sexuality while taking distress, harm and responsibility seriously.

What the current diagnosis means

People sometimes use the phrases sex addiction or hypersexuality when sexual behaviour feels difficult to control. Those everyday labels are not interchangeable with a clinical diagnosis. The World Health Organization’s ICD-11 includes compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, or CSBD, under impulse-control disorders, with the code 6C72.

The central concern is a persistent loss of control over repetitive sexual behaviour that causes substantial distress or interferes with important parts of life. Clinicians look for a pattern over an extended period, typically six months or more. Someone does not need to wait six months to ask for help when a problem is already affecting safety or wellbeing.

The DSM-5-TR does not list sex addiction as a separate diagnosis. This difference between classification systems does not mean that a person’s difficulties are imaginary or untreatable. Equally, describing the problem as exactly the same as alcohol or opioid addiction goes beyond what the evidence establishes. A careful assessment is more useful than choosing a label first.

High desire, private behaviour and moral guilt are different

A strong interest in sex is not, by itself, a disorder. Neither a particular number of partners nor masturbation, pornography use or frequency of consensual sex can establish CSBD on its own. What matters is impaired control and meaningful consequences, understood in the person’s wider circumstances.

Distress that comes entirely from moral or religious disapproval of otherwise controlled sexual behaviour is not sufficient for this diagnosis. That distress can still deserve respectful support. A therapist should help you understand it without automatically declaring your sexuality an addiction or dismissing beliefs that matter to you.

Sexual orientation, a consensual preference, or a mismatch in partners’ desire is not proof of CSBD. Paraphilic disorders are a separate diagnostic area and must not be casually equated with compulsive sexual behaviour. Assessment should consider consent and harm accurately, without turning differences in sexuality into evidence of illness.

Patterns that can make an assessment worthwhile

A useful question is whether you can make and follow choices about sexual behaviour. Repeated attempts to cut back may fail, activities may take over time needed for work or family, or the behaviour may continue despite health, financial or relationship consequences. Some people keep repeating it even when it brings little satisfaction.

The pattern might involve online sexual activity, pornography, masturbation or encounters with other people. These are possible settings for a problem, not a checklist of inherently unhealthy activities. The same behaviour can have very different meanings depending on control, consent, context and impact.

Secrecy and guilt can accompany difficulties but are not diagnostic tests. Privacy is normal, and shame can occur without a disorder. It may help to write down what happens, what you have tried to change, and the concrete consequences. Take that account to a qualified clinician instead of relying on a quiz that diagnoses addiction from frequency alone.

Consider health, relationships and responsibility together

Loss of control can affect sleep, concentration, finances, emotional wellbeing and relationships. Depending on the behaviour, there may also be concerns about sexually transmitted infections or pregnancy. The relevant risks should be discussed individually; not everyone seeking help has the same experiences or needs.

If trust has been damaged, naming a health problem does not cancel responsibility for choices or oblige a partner to accept further harm. Support can include individual therapy, clear boundaries and, where both people want it and it is appropriate, relationship work. A partner’s needs deserve attention in their own right.

Consent remains necessary in every interaction. Treatment is not about persuading a reluctant partner to provide more sex or making someone else responsible for controlling your behaviour. Where sexual-health care is relevant, ask about testing, contraception and prevention. These practical steps can be taken while the underlying difficulties are assessed.

What a professional assessment should explore

Look for a licensed mental-health professional with experience in sexual health and compulsive behaviour. A primary-care clinician can help with a referral. The conversation may cover the pattern over time, what feels out of control, impact on daily life, previous attempts to change and what you hope treatment will achieve.

Other explanations or co-occurring problems matter. Mood episodes, including mania, alcohol or drug effects, some neurological conditions and certain medicines can change sexual behaviour. Depression, anxiety and other difficulties may also need care. A sudden change after a new medicine or alongside major mood changes should be mentioned promptly; do not stop prescribed treatment on your own.

You can ask how the clinician handles confidentiality, how they distinguish high desire from impaired control and whether their approach respects sexual diversity. If involving a partner or family member is proposed, clarify the purpose and consent arrangements. An assessment should produce a useful care plan, not just a label.

Therapy can build control without treating sexuality as the enemy

Treatment commonly includes psychological therapy. Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, can help identify situations and emotions linked to a problematic pattern, develop alternative responses and make realistic plans for difficult moments. Other approaches may address acceptance, values, emotional regulation or relationship difficulties according to need.

There is treatment research, although it is still limited. A 2019 randomised study involving 137 men found support for a seven-week group CBT programme compared with waiting for treatment. It studied a proposed hypersexual-disorder definition, so its results do not establish that one programme works for every person diagnosed under current ICD-11 criteria.

A suitable goal is better control, functioning and sexual wellbeing, with behaviour that respects consent and personal choices. Complete lifelong abstinence from all sexual activity is not a universal clinical requirement. Agree specific goals with the therapist and review whether treatment is improving your life, rather than measuring progress only by a rigid count of sexual events.

Medicines are selected for an individual plan

A clinician may consider medication alongside therapy, particularly when another condition also needs treatment. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, and naltrexone are among medicines discussed in specialist guidance for selected adults with CSBD. Their use for this purpose is generally off-label, and evidence remains limited.

An antidepressant may be considered when depression, anxiety or obsessive symptoms are part of the picture, but that does not mean everyone with difficult sexual behaviour needs one. Naltrexone also has specific precautions and interactions. The prescriber should explain the reason for choosing a medicine, expected benefits, adverse effects and follow-up.

Do not use someone else’s prescription, buy a libido-suppressing product online or change doses to blunt sexual feelings. Treatment should not simply aim to eliminate desire at any cost. Discuss unwanted sexual effects and other side effects openly; the balance between benefit and harm needs ongoing review.

Support groups and intensive programmes are options, not requirements

Some people find peer support helpful, including groups that use a twelve-step model such as Sex Addicts Anonymous. A group may offer a place to talk, reduce isolation and practise agreed changes. It is an optional support, not proof of a diagnosis and not a replacement for assessment when significant mental-health or safety concerns are present.

Groups differ in language, beliefs, privacy rules and goals. Ask what participation involves and whether the approach fits your needs. Claims that one group or abstinence rule is the only route to recovery should be treated cautiously. Evidence for specific peer programmes is less developed than advertising can suggest.

Residential or inpatient treatment is not automatically required, and there is no universal thirty-day minimum programme. The appropriate setting depends on severity, immediate safety, other conditions and available outpatient support. Before committing to an intensive programme, ask about staff qualifications, the treatment plan, costs and continuing care after discharge.

Make progress practical and know when to seek urgent help

A plan can include noticing early warning signs, reducing access to situations that repeatedly lead to harm, building other ways to manage distress and arranging follow-up. Choose practical steps with your therapist rather than punitive rules that increase secrecy or shame. A setback is information for revising the plan, not a reason to abandon care.

Improvement may involve better sleep, reliable work and family routines, fewer harmful episodes, stronger boundaries and more confidence in making choices. There is no single recovery timetable. If treatment is not helping, discuss whether the diagnosis, goals, approach or an untreated co-occurring condition needs another look.

Seek urgent professional help if you think you may harm yourself or another person, cannot keep someone safe, or are in an acute mental-health crisis. Otherwise, you can begin with a routine appointment before consequences become more serious. Asking for help is compatible with taking responsibility and with preserving a healthy, consensual sexual life.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current ICD-11 recognises CSBD as an impulse-control disorder; the DSM-5-TR does not list sex addiction as a separate diagnosis.

High desire, consensual variation or distress based entirely on moral disapproval does not by itself establish CSBD.

Therapy has supportive but still developing evidence; medicines and treatment intensity need individual clinical decisions.

How BeMama can help

Describe the pattern and its practical effects, seek a qualified clinician and agree goals that improve control, relationships and wellbeing.

When to seek help

If there is an immediate risk of harm to yourself or another person, contact emergency or urgent mental-health support. Seek professional advice for sudden behaviour changes, and do not alter prescribed medicines without guidance.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A diagnosis depends on persistent impaired control and distress or functional harm, not a sexual-frequency threshold.
  • Moral guilt and relationship disagreements may need support without being CSBD.
  • Assessment should consider other health conditions, medicines and substance effects.
  • Treatment aims for safer choices, improved functioning and healthy sexuality.
  • Peer groups, medication and residential care are options for selected needs, not universal requirements.

Frequently asked questions

Is sex addiction an official diagnosis?

Terminology differs. ICD-11 recognises compulsive sexual behaviour disorder as an impulse-control disorder. DSM-5-TR does not list sex addiction as a separate diagnosis.

Does a high sex drive mean I have CSBD?

No. High desire alone does not establish a disorder. Assessment focuses on persistent impaired control and substantial distress or interference with life.

Can guilt alone establish the diagnosis?

No. Distress arising entirely from moral or religious disapproval is not enough for CSBD. You can still seek support for that distress.

Does pornography use or masturbation automatically count?

No. These activities do not establish a diagnosis by themselves. Context, control, consequences and consent matter.

Is CSBD the same as a paraphilic disorder?

No. They are distinct clinical concepts and require careful assessment. Sexual orientation or consensual preferences do not establish either diagnosis.

Do I have to wait six months before asking for help?

No. Diagnostic assessment considers a sustained pattern, but you can seek support as soon as behaviour is causing concern or harm.

Is there evidence that therapy can help?

Yes, although the research is still developing. CBT has supportive trial findings, with limits in the populations and diagnostic definitions studied.

Will treatment require me to stop all sexual activity forever?

No. Complete lifelong abstinence is not a universal requirement. Goals should address control, wellbeing, consent and the problems identified in assessment.

Does everyone need medication or residential treatment?

No. Treatment is individual. Therapy is commonly used, while medicines or intensive care depend on severity, other conditions, safety and clinical judgement.

Can a partner be responsible for managing the behaviour?

No. A partner can choose to offer support, but consent and personal boundaries remain essential. Treatment does not remove responsibility for choices or obligate someone to stay in a harmful situation.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
